speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prince Albert):
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TWO-DAY DEBATE ON INTERNATIONAL SITUATION-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In view of the increasingly alarming situation in which freedom finds itself today in Europe, Africa and Asia, as freedom-loving nations are falling under the domination of the U.S.S.R. and its satellites, and with the massive Soviet military expansion posing a frightening threat to the west, which a few days ago was described by the former prime minister of the United Kingdom, the Right Honourable Harold Macmillan, in these words, "The Soviet Union seems to get away with anything, just like Hitler got away with anything", in my opinion Canadians and the western world generally have a false sense of security. Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski):
That before the dissolution of parliament, two days should be set aside for the discussion of the terrifying international situation and the need for action to be recommended and taken by Canada to meet the situation in so far as our country is concerned, before it may be too late.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under Standing Order 43 and seek the unanimous consent of the House to discuss a motion relating to a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Given the fact that since January 1, 1979 an agreement between Canada and the United States forbids any Canadian who has a police record of some kind to stay in the United States unless he obtains a special authorization certificate; that such an agreement is a direct breach of individual rights and liberties; and that it uselessly penalizes law abiding citizens who have had the misfortune of making one mistake, however small, in their life, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Allard):

As he knows, the Centre for the Study of Inflation and Productivity, yesterday and the business pages of the press in most cities across Canada, today demonstrated astronomically high increases in the profits of corporations and, therefore, in the prices of almost every sector of the Canadian economy.
Considering that almost every Canadian makes a purchase from one of the large department stores, and considering specifically that their profits went up some 89 per cent-we know what that means for prices-will the Prime Minister take some concrete action and call in, for example, the head of Simpsons-Sears, the head of Hudson's Bay-

The point remains, however, that there are profits, sometimes substantial profits, in various sectors. Members on this side have indicated their reaction to it and this is my reaction: we are glad that there are profits. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: REQUEST THAT HEADS OF LARGE CORPORATIONS GIVE COMMITMENTS TO HOLD DOWN PRICES AND PROFITS
speechtext: Order, please.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT HEADS OF LARGE CORPORATIONS GIVE COMMITMENTS TO HOLD DOWN PRICES AND PROFITS
speechtext: Considering that wage and salary increases last year, in 1978, for Canadian workers were only up slightly more than 6 per cent, and considering that a couple of weeks ago the Prime Minister lectured women bank clerks, who are amongst the worst paid in the country, is he now saying to the people of Canada that firms such as those in the retail sector which have had astronomical profit increases well beyond their increase in sales are justified in that course of action, and is he going to defend unlimited profits and attack ordinary workers who want a decent income? Is that what he is saying?

subtopic: REQUEST THAT HEADS OF LARGE CORPORATIONS GIVE COMMITMENTS TO HOLD DOWN PRICES AND PROFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member talks about attacking ordinary workers and lecturing bank clerks. I put it

to him that he has said this a few times and that he is distorting the facts. He may, in his tunnel vision, not understand what I have been saying; I will repeat it. But surely that is not what I said.
I said that it is good there are profits, and that it is important those profits be used to create growth in the economy. I said inside this House, outside this House and when I met with the business leaders, that it is of great concern to the government that having made profits-which shows progress in the growth of the economy-they not be used just for the benefit of the shareholders, but that the corporations have a responsibility to see that the distribution of those profits is for the good of all Canadians. Apart from the shareholders, the corporations have to consider the consumers, the workers and the growth of the enterprise itself. In other words, they must reinvest the profits to make more jobs for more Canadians. That is the position of the government. We are not apologetic about profits; we are glad that there are profits.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT HEADS OF LARGE CORPORATIONS GIVE COMMITMENTS TO HOLD DOWN PRICES AND PROFITS
speechtext: We don't need a lecture on economics.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT HEADS OF LARGE CORPORATIONS GIVE COMMITMENTS TO HOLD DOWN PRICES AND PROFITS
speechtext: We are very happy that the workers can get increased wages as a result of those profits. What we are saying is that the corporations should not expect, if they are going to give increased wages to their workers and increased dividends to their shareholders, to be able to turn around and get increased prices from the consumers just as a result of their largesse to themselves.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT HEADS OF LARGE CORPORATIONS GIVE COMMITMENTS TO HOLD DOWN PRICES AND PROFITS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the Prime Minister's long answer he made one of his red herring accusations. He knows as well as I that this party has never opposed unreasonable profits.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT HEADS OF LARGE CORPORATIONS GIVE COMMITMENTS TO HOLD DOWN PRICES AND PROFITS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: REQUEST THAT HEADS OF LARGE CORPORATIONS GIVE COMMITMENTS TO HOLD DOWN PRICES AND PROFITS
speechtext:
I notice that the Prime Minister is smiling. He is aware of my point that, for example, we have governed in the province of Saskatchewan which has the lowest cost government in this country, per capita, and it favours reasonable profits.
Considering that in the United States both President Kennedy and President Johnson, when they saw that the steel sector was making more than reasonable profits and indulging in price-gouging, called the companies in and forced them to reduce their prices and profits. What I am asking, in this context, is that the Prime Minister put up or shut up. Will he do the same in this country on behalf of Canadian consumers?

subtopic: REQUEST THAT HEADS OF LARGE CORPORATIONS GIVE COMMITMENTS TO HOLD DOWN PRICES AND PROFITS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the New Democratic Party said that his party has never opposed unreasonable profits; is that right?

subtopic: REQUEST THAT HEADS OF LARGE CORPORATIONS GIVE COMMITMENTS TO HOLD DOWN PRICES AND PROFITS
speechtext: Reasonable profits.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT HEADS OF LARGE CORPORATIONS GIVE COMMITMENTS TO HOLD DOWN PRICES AND PROFITS
speechtext: So he is opposed to reasonable ones?

subtopic: REQUEST THAT HEADS OF LARGE CORPORATIONS GIVE COMMITMENTS TO HOLD DOWN PRICES AND PROFITS
speechtext:
Oh, oh!
February 7, 1979

Oral Questions

The hon. member has gone back into the history of President Kennedy and others and has said that they called in the steel industry. We did the very same thing: we set up the Estey commission, called in the steel industry and had an inquiry to which they responded. The hon. member did not like the report, but that is what we did.
I repeat the position of the government: the profits are welcome, but it is important that those who get the profit consider that the Canadian economic society as a whole has helped them to make that profit and, therefore, it should not only be for their shareholders nor, indeed, for their workers. If the workers can get an increased share of the profits, that is fine with the government. We just do not want these companies or corporations, particularly those which are regulated, to seek to justify higher rates by saying, "We need more money and we shall get it out of the consumer or make these profits". That is the position of the government. I should like to hear the Leader of the NDP state his position with regard to these profits.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT POLICY ON DISPOSAL OF CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the President of the Treasury Board. In Monday's Ottawa Journal, the president of Air Canada is quoted as saying that the government is considering selling Air Canada to the private sector. In that article, Mr. Taylor gave several good reasons why the government might make this decision.
February 7, 1979

In view of the fact these reasons could apply equally well to other Crown corporations, is the government prepared, or is it considering divesting itself of and selling off some of the 400-odd Crown corporations it now possesses?

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT POLICY ON DISPOSAL OF CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, to the best of my knowledge, the government has made no decision at this time to sell of any of its present Crown corporations.

speechtext:

subsubtopic: PASSING OF SALES TAX CUT TO CONSUMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. In November, the government cut the manufacturing sales tax by 3 per cent and, in essence, handed over $1 billion to the corporations. Statistics Canada said today the industry selling price index for manufacturing was up 10 per cent this year over last year.
The minister said on January 23 when we questioned him in the House that he would look into this matter to see whether or not the sales tax cut was passed on to consumers. Can the minister tell the House what specific action the government is taking to make sure the sales tax cut is passed to consumers as intended?

speakeroldname: Hon. Warren Allmand (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: PASSING OF SALES TAX CUT TO CONSUMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I pointed out when I answered the question on a previous occasion, the inventories that are benefiting from the tax cut only came on the market about the middle of January; they were not on the market before Christmas, as alleged in the question the hon. member put earlier and as the Canadian Consumers' Association alleged.
Since these inventories came on the market only recently, we are watching them closely through the 50 offices of our department across the country, and by working with CSIP which has the analytical manpower to analyse any situation which seems to be out of line. Thus far, we have received very few complaints with respect to the fact that the cuts are not being passed on.
I might say that prior to the end of the year the AIB wrote to all of the companies reporting to it, asking how they intended to pass on this tax cut. That information was provided to the Minister of Finance. Most companies set out their plans. We are watching the situation closely now. So far we have had no information that they are not, but it is too early to judge.

subsubtopic: PASSING OF SALES TAX CUT TO CONSUMERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, again I ask the minister what mechanism the government is going to set up to make sure that this is enforced. analysis, whether the cut is being passed on or not. If it is not being passed on, we intend to make that public, jawbone, and press for the passing on of the tax cut.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I presented a budget on November 16 last which gave a lot of stimulus to the industrial sector in order to make it more competitive. speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: STEPS TO NARROW CURRENT ACCOUNT DEFICIT
speechtext: My question to the minister is this. The governor indicated he has done as much as he thinks he can do with regard to monetary policy. subtopic: STEPS TO NARROW CURRENT ACCOUNT DEFICIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the governor is not called upon to make comments on fiscal policy. He said that if I were to accept the proposition of the hon. member-the professor-who has indicated we should have a lower interest rate, the effect would be to have a weaker dollar. The governor said there is some alternative. We could raise taxes. At the same time, he said that if we were to do that, it would have a negative effect on the economy.
Fiscal policy calls for judgments. We have made them. The economy is doing much better. If I were to follow the phantom deficit policies of the opposition, the dollar would be lower than ever. I think we have followed the best policy possible at this time. That is why many sectors of the Canadian economy have been operating at full capacity.

subtopic: STEPS TO NARROW CURRENT ACCOUNT DEFICIT

USE OF EARTH STATIONS BY CABLE TV OPERATORS IN REMOTE AREAS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Communications. In view of the announced plans of the Department of Communications to experiment with individual roof-type earth stations on some homes in certain rural areas of Canada, can the minister tell the House whether this experiment may also be broadened in such a way as to allow cable TV operators in isolated areas such as northern Ontario to utilize suitable earth stations and thereby provide a much wider range of TV viewing choices to their subscribers?

subtopic: USE OF EARTH STATIONS BY CABLE TV OPERATORS IN REMOTE AREAS
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, that kind of experiment is designed precisely to allow people in remote areas to receive broadcast signals directly from the satellite to their homes. The reason Canada developed that particular technology through the Hermes satellite was in order to allow remote areas of the country to participate in the full development of this country.
However, at the present time, there is a need for more considerable use of the satellite for broadcasting, and cable operators and others are actively putting together broadcast programs for it. When this is done, the liberalization of the earth station policy will help all these regions to acquire this service at relatively low cost. The answer to the hon. member's question, in short, is that that is exactly the purpose of the experiment.
What substantive evidence does the minister have to give us that that is a fact, that the Canadian dollar is only temporarily low at the present time?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are many people in the world who think that the Canadian dollar represents a figure that is undervalued and is, therefore, very attractive. In speaking to the forest products industry and quoting their own views, in making serious decisions about investments down the track and plants to come on stream two, three or five years hence, they quite wisely would prefer not to count on what I think is a temporary competitive advantage related to the Canadian dollar.
It is a very logical argument that they share, that they do not want to make forward investments of the magnitude that are required, in the neighbourhood of $3 billion, over the next five to seven years on that assumption.

subsubtopic: POSTAL WORKERS WHOM MINISTER WOULD FIRE-UNION AFFILIATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Postmaster General. The House will recall that the last time I asked him a question regarding what he felt was a need to fire some 500 postal workers in order to bring about efficiency in the Post Office, the minister wiffled and waffled: he said the number could be 100 or 1,000.
I do not want to charge the minister with seeking sensational press in order to antagonize unions or bamboozle the public, so I will ask him to come clean with the Canadian public. Has the minister a list of such persons and, if he does, does he know the unions to which they belong? That is a simple question which does not call for any long, rhetorical answers, which is what I usually get.

subsubtopic: POSTAL WORKERS WHOM MINISTER WOULD FIRE-UNION AFFILIATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think I can answer the question, because of the way it was put. The hon. member for Hamilton West is a lawyer from a working town, and I would like to take this

February 7, 1979
Oral Questions
occasion to correct what he said the other day on a point of order. Ele said that the Post Office is under a closed shop status. There is no such thing as a closed shop at the Post Office. Postal workers are covered by the Rand formula, and that is the information I must give the hon. member. If they were covered by a closed shop, every time a union suspends a postal worker we would have to suspend him from work at the same time, and this is what CUPW has asked.
With regard to the 500 workers we are supposed to fire, I gave an answer to that the other day which I think was very simple. In a telephone conversation with the media, I said the number could be 100, 500 or 1,000. My job is not to defend workers or management; my job is to see that both fulfil their responsibilities, and that is the job I am doing at the moment.

subsubtopic: POSTAL WORKERS WHOM MINISTER WOULD FIRE-UNION AFFILIATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 think I can now charge the minister with seeking sensational press in order to antagonize the unions and bamboozle the public. I related to the minister reports of pilfering, smoking pot, drinking and goofing off, and these reports have not been challenged. The reports indicate that the minister finds that he cannot correct these situations because of the rules.
Is the minister now telling the Canadian people that because of present rules, supervisors and managers find their hands are tied and that they are unable to manage efficiently and effectively? In other words, what is the sense of having a department if it cannot be controlled?

subsubtopic: POSTAL WORKERS WHOM MINISTER WOULD FIRE-UNION AFFILIATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member should know that we live in a democracy and not under a dictatorship. We try to see that our workers work well, but when we see headlines in the newspapers such as the one we saw this morning, "Post Office ordered to rehire two accused of drug trafficking", we have to accept judges' decisions in these matters. We do not like it, but we have to accept them. We have to abide by the rules of democracy.
However, as far as I am concerned, there is no backing off. If postal workers do not want to fulfil their responsibilities, and if they do not want to work honestly, we will see that they get out of the Post Office.

The House resumed from Monday, February 5, consideration of the motion of Miss Begin that Bill C-2, to amend the Health Resources Fund Act, be read the third time and do pass.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak on Bill C-2, the Health Resources Fund Act, which is to help provinces build better health training facilities. I see this bill as a microcosm of the problems we face in our country today. Here is a bill that came about as a result of a commitment which the federal government made to the provinces some 13 years ago. The particular agreement has another two years of life left in it. Before the time limit expired, the government withdrew its commitment and said, "We are going to terminate it before it is finished". That is a microcosm of the problems we face in the country today.
Yesterday the first ministers completed their meeting which was held just across the street from Parliament Hill. It was evident from watching and listening to the proceedings that one of the greatest problems we face today is associated with trust. The Canadian public has no confidence in the government because it has had too many successive agreements with provincial governments which have been broken before the ink dried. Perhaps the government can justify itself and say that the life of the agreement has been almost spent. Nevertheless, it is the principle of the thing. As the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk) pointed out, the government unilaterally breaks agreements and cuts off the funding to the provinces.
Because of this example, when a provincial minister of health enters into any new agreement with the federal government, he becomes somewhat gun shy. That was evident on television yesterday when we watched the first ministers taking part in their discussions. The fundamental problem was that we cannot accept the word of the government at face value. We do not know how long an agreement will last. Will the government unilaterally cut off an agreement when it sees fit? Once the government has received what it wants out of a bargain, will it cut off its share of the funding? It is a typically centralist view of the government that it will establish a
Health Resources Fund Act
program because the omniscient central government knows best what should be happening across the country. It knows what the health standards ought to be in each of the provinces. Thus, the government designs a policy for the provinces, helps to fund it, and after a few years when the provincial governments are depending upon that funding and are hooked, unilaterally the federal government withdraws. No provincial government wants to enter into agreements of any kind with the federal government when that happens.
Having seen what the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) tabled in the House, naturally I was very interested in the speech she made in Vancouver. I have a copy of the minister's speech which was made on January 16, 1979 to the Association of Professional Economists of British Columbia. It is entitled: "The Prophets of Doom are Wrong". The last paragraph on page one reads as follows:
A favourite expression of the prophets of gloom and doom is "conservative backlash". Okay, let's look at this idea. The truth is that people don't like paying taxes, and when they do pay them, like to see that the money is well spent. So far, so good. That's as it should be. But people do not want us to cut down on government services, and in particular they don't want us to cut back on health and welfare benefits. On the contrary, Canadians welcome each new move to improve these benefits. I have heard this not once but hundreds of times from people across the country. What Canadians are saying loud and clear is that they have confidence in the future of this country. The difficulties of these past few years have not diminished their pride and compassion.
I should like to underscore the following sentence:
But people do not want us to cut down on government services, and in particular they don't want us to cut back on health and welfare benefits.
That is what the minister said in Vancouver, but she did not tell those economists that legislation cutting back on health research programs in the provinces had been tabled in the House. The minister cannot have it both ways. She should have said in Vancouver the same thing she said here. The minister's distemper is showing somewhat, and I do not blame her; but at least she could do the House and Canada a service by being consistent in her statements.
At page 2 the address continued:
Some of the blame for this current of reactionary hysteria has to be taken by the official opposition in parliament.
I want to remind the minister that it was not the official opposition which tabled this bill. The official opposition did not cut off the $83 million to the provinces. The official opposition did not make the announcement last August 1 which led to this legislation. Yet the minister wants to blame the official opposition for the legislation. The minister continued:
What makes the opposition's role troubling is, first, that they are highly visible, and second, that I don't think they are being completely candid.
I suggest that is the pot calling the kettle black. I remind the minister that perhaps one of the functions of the opposition is to be highly visible, especially concerning issues such as this one when the minister is not dealing candidly with Canadians. A few months from now when the minister is on this side of the House, she will know what it is like and she will do the same thing.

We will have a majority.
February 7, 1979

Health Resources Fund Act

The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson) will be dancing to another tune in a few months.
At page 6 of the minister's address, this appears:
Poverty isn't as blatant as it was when I taught school in a poor neighbourhood in Montreal. But it is there all the same. When medical researchers looked into conditions-
Because of the legislation being brought forward by the government, very soon there will be no medical researchers in Canada; they are going south. In fact, doctors are leaving my constituency and going to Portland because they want some freedom in which to operate; I do not mean that as a pun. Canada now places something like fourteenth among western countries in its commitment to any kind of research, yet the government has introduced more cutbacks. The minister will not have to worry very long because there will be no medical researchers left in the country. The address continued as follows:
When medical researchers looked into conditions in a single poor school district in Montreal a short while back they found that 21 per cent of the kids were retarded in physical development, 28 per cent retarded in physical-mental co-ordination, 39 per cent had family histories of diabetes and 20 per cent had family histories of tuberculosis. These are things you can measure scientifically, but there are harder to measure troubles for poor kids ranging from violent crime to depression to early death or suicide.
I agree that those are problems requiring attention. Pray tell, why is the minister cutting back funding which would provide for greater medical research in the province of Quebec? Such research would help the people who are facing the crises to which the minister referred. The illogical position in which the minister has placed herself staggers the imagination. On the one hand she said that we have inhuman medical problems in the schoolyards of our provinces. On the other hand she said that the government will cut back on medical research funding to the provinces. This cutback means that the provinces will not be able to provide the necessary health services to reduce illnesses.
At page 6 the last paragraph reads as follows:
The government did not feel it could wait for better times to take action. We began with the knowledge that the three major federal programs for children were weighted in favour of upper income families. These programs-the family allowances, child tax exemptions, and the $50 tax credit-actually brought more benefits to families with incomes of $50,000 than to families earning less than $5,000.
The money diverted from the federal coffers to the provincial coffers to be invested in medical research became somewhat anonymous. One really could not identify which dollars were federal, provincial or from private industry. There was not enough of a visible label for people to identify this as money coming from the federal government.
As the minister said, the government could not stand idly by, so rather than having that money come from the federal government to the provinces anonymously the government found a way by which it could be identified as coming from the Liberal government. What the government did was cut back on the family allowance from $28 to $20 and institute a child tax credit program. Now every family in the country

knows when it gets that $200 cheque, or the $20 a month, not computing the amount on their little pocket calculators and, therefore, not realizing they are getting no more than before, that this money is coming from the federal government. The government hopes they will show their gratitude to the federal government at the next federal election now that the unanimity has been erased. People in Quebec, British Columbia, Saskatchewan, P.E.I. and Newfoundland will know when they receive these cheques, supposedly to help with their medical problems, that the money is coming gratuitously from the federal government. I know the people of Canada are sufficiently sophisticated that they will know this is an attempt to buy them, and they will not allow themselves to be bought in that way. They will just not allow that to happen.
I recall that just a few weeks ago, before the Christmas break, the minister had an interchange with the hon. member for Athabasca regarding health services for Indians. She said that Indians were not going to lose any of the medical benefits to which they were accustomed. I happen to know that if you go to some of the ridings in British Columbia you will find that native Indians have indeed lost some of the medical services to which they have been accustomed. I know that clinics have been shut down because of inadequate funding. Because these clinics now do not have sufficient staffs, this department is flying nurses into the areas. Given the kind of weather they experience along the course-

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. speechtext: No, that is not true.

I notice that the Minister of National Health and Welfare is getting her prompting from the Minister of State (Environment) (Mr. Marchand). Obviously she was occupied in trying to make sure the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Stollery) received enough help to get re-elected, and now that she knows that is not going to work she has entered into a discussion with that minister and is taking his prompting in order to enter into this discussion. That is not the responsibility of the province of British Columbia, it is the responsibility of her department. Let me give one illustration. The hospital at Bella Coola was condemned four years ago. I was there a couple of years ago and some of the concerned people living there showed me that hospital. The United Church of Canada started that mission many years ago and performed wonderful and valiant services in the area. That hospital is staffed by people with a kind of pioneer spirit who like that frontier work. They are committed to helping the people. However, the hospital building has been condemned for four years. The minister says she has not cut back on the services to these people.
The hon. member for Coast Chilcotin (Mr. Pearsall) is not in the House, but he has not been running to their aid. The minister who is now promoting herself as the "minister of professional sports" has not been coming to the aid of these people. This hospital is understaffed and the people are not being looked after, yet this minister is content to cut back on these funds and this kind of service, leaving these people unattended.
There are people in my riding who can well use the research money provided by this fund. Let me name two of them. The Variety's Treatment Centre for Children, is a tremendous facility that is funded through the efforts of the people in the lower mainland. There are in the neighbourhood of 300 families whose children are being helped and given treatment in this very beautiful facility. These are children with cerebral palsy, muscular dystrophy and so on. This centre is not getting the kind of income tax break from this government it deserves in order to help those children. This Variety's Treatment Centre for Children could certainly use more research money in order to provide better treatment, yet the government wants to cut back on research facilities of this kind.
We have another facility, namely, the Seagull Centre. It uses a relatively new technique to help paraplegics and quadriplegics with motor problems. A machine has been designed that helps in a mechanical way to get the limbs of these people in motion. By this method it is possible that they can again become workers through the reduction or elimination of their paralysis. Several groups working in the lower mainland are using this method in their clinics. If the federal government were to continue funding in this field of research, hopefully help could be provided to these people who suffer from paralysis in their legs and/or arms. The minister is really not doing any service at all to the people of Canada by cutting back on these funds.
Let me go back to what I said at the outset. This problem is one that involves not just funding, although that is a very important and immediate concern. This problem is one that involves trust. How many times do we have to come to this government asking it to live up to its commitments? This agreement was supposed to continue for longer, but this government is unilaterally cutting back on funds, breaking its agreement with the Canadian people. That is the problem we face in this country, and that breach of faith is well illustrated and documented by the legislation we are debating today.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate today to touch on an area which in the
Health Resources Fund Act
past has not received the attention it deserves. I welcome the opportunity to bring some of our problems to the attention of members in this House.
Let me make a prediction. I suggest that 20 years from now there will be an older group of members in this House of Commons than we see today, because Canada's population at this time is an aging population. I say this because last Sunday in the town of Penetanguishene I attended a birthday party for a man named Michael Asselin, who was 95 years of age. He met me at the door. He is a very capable fellow and speaks both English and French, but mostly English. I was amazed at his wisdom. He had been raised in that area, was still able to walk and talk and he said to me that he still liked to dance with the ladies. This is the type of individual we are running into today.
As a matter of interest, it so happens that this man's forebears fought at the battle of Hastings in the Norman conquest of 1066, and a tombstone to a Lord Asselin can be found in England today. This gentleman grew up in French surroundings in the area of Perkins Field and Lafontaine. At various points in his life this man was a councillor, the reeve of his township, a warden of the county and the secretary-treasurer of his riding. He ran again for the position of reeve at age 78. People felt that he was too old, but he got elected and performed one of the best jobs as reeve ever done in that riding.
After that birthday party I went back to my home town of Orillia to the Free Methodist Church there and attended the celebration of two people, one who was 90 years of age and another who was 93 years of age. They were both walking around and shaking hands with the guests. I tell these stories to illustrate the point that people are living longer and healthier because of the prevention of infectious diseases in their youth or middle age.
I would like to go back to the turn of the century to further illustrate my point to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin). There were two major scientific events before the year 1900, the breakthrough by Pasteur who found that organisms cause disease, and Lister's invention of antiseptic therapy in surgery. His carbolic spray cut down mortality.
In those times doctors came to the house, sat by the bedside and brought comfort and many times spiritual help, faith, hope and courage to people for the future. In that way they raised their patient's hopes psychologically in the hope that they would recover from their illness. The doctors in those days knew their patients intimately. Today the doctor walks into a ward accompanied by para-medical personnel, stops at one patient and gives him an examination, talks about him and then goes on to the next. There is no real contact with the patient.
In earlier days we also had infectious diseases such as scarlet fever, diphtheria, pneumonia, pernicious anemia and diabetes, which were rampant. I am sure that many doctors in this House have never seen a case of pernicious anemia. These

February 7, 1979
Health Resources Fund Act
were the diseases which killed in the early 1900s. Infections were the big killers up to 1935. If hon. members would like to take time out and are feeling a little spiritual and thinking about what may happen to them, I suggest that they go through old cemetery. What they will find are the tombstones of whole groups of children who died from diphtheria or infectious diseases simply because doctors had nothing to offer them.
The first diphtheria antitoxin used in the province of Ontario was in 1905. There were big families at that particular time. I can recall a family of 13 children, five of which died from diphtheria. That was the tragedy of those days, to see these infections hit whole communities. A similar disease was scarlet fever, but fortunately they developed antitoxins and from there they developed toxoids. We were well on the way to wiping out infectious diseases.
The discovery of insulin by Banting and Best in 1924 saved the lives of many young children who would have died before their twenties. I knew a young doctor by the name of Gilchrist who had diabetes in his youth, but went on to medical school and became an authority on that very disease. Two scientists by the names of Minot and Murphy at the University of Chicago discovered the cause of pernicious anemia, which was vitamin B-12. After that there was one discovery after another. Sulfa drugs were developed and used to control streptococcus. Penicillin was discovered and first used during the war in 1942. It was discovered quite accidentally from a mould.
This story of the field of medicine is intensely fascinating, and if I had the time I would tell some of it to hon. members, but time does not permit me to do so. There is the story of the golden antibiotics and what they did to curb pneumonia and other diseases. The mortality rate from pneumonia in the early 1940s was approximately 25 per cent. In most of the cases it was the breadwinner who perished, fellows who were out roughing it, leaving behind a widow with four or five children and no source of income. Today, however, pneumonia is considered a secondary disease with a mortality rate of between 3 and 5 per cent.
The next major disease was polio. It was found that it was an infectious virus carried by elements of the environment. It was very interesting at that time to note that the cleaner one became, the more paralysing polio became, particularly to people between 20 and 30 years of age. I saw many people die with respiratory paralysis before the development of the iron lung. I saw it in epidemic proportions. I can remember seeing a young girl being examined and the doctor saying not to turn her over because she would not be able to breathe. She died from respiratory paralysis.
The sadness and tragedy of all this was cured because of the research which was put into polio; and it returned millions of dollars of dividends on every dollar which was spent on it, so let us have no argument on that score. I know the minister will take this all to heart and immediately start hunting for more research money.

Now here we have a group of younger people coming around and they are getting older. Then we found out a new thing. We were running into chronic diseases. We were running into coronaries, we were running into cardiovascular disease, we were running into strokes, and those are disabling or total. We were running into maturity onset diabetes and many other diseases, arthritis particularly. Those were things that were crippling people in their fifties with a great deal of knowledge. I have learned one thing in getting old, and I thank the Lord for that. I remember that when I graduated at 31 I thought I had the world before me and knew it all, only to learn at my age that I know less and less. This is something we must keep in mind.
So here we have all these people with cardiovascular and chronic diseases. I do not want to make reference to anybody in the Chair, but you will know, sir, about cardiovascular surgery and the good it has done for thousands of people across this land, enabling them to go back to work and take their place in society, receiving pay for it and paying taxes, not only into the pension plan but to the government to keep things going and help the people who are less healthy. This is what we are doing with the research funds we have had to date.
But we have only begun, because our aging population today will bring about the need for increased care. Today there are well over two million people in Canada over the age of 65, and by 1990 there will probably be three million. Those people will go on pension. They will be drawing old age pensions but there will be a smaller group of people in the work force to pay those pensions. Here we come back to our problem. What we have to do is educate a new group of doctors who will be trained in the difference and the clinical values of chronic disease and how this can be handled. I hope the minister appreciates how important and necessary it is to train geriatric doctors who will understand these illnesses among people who are 50 years of age and over. I shall not go further into this aspect because I do not have time but there are a lot of differences between symptoms presented by a person between 55 and 75 and those of people aged 25 or 35 or 40 or 50. I could give a long list of differences which exist.
We have trained doctors who really do not relish the idea of looking at that old patient lying there in a bed who is crippled, who cannot move, who maybe has suffered a stroke. Maybe they need some treatment. Maybe they need physiotherapy. But it always seems to me that this is the case no matter what hospital I am in. I noticed it in my own clinic; there was only one doctor besides myself who made and enjoyed calls in general on these patients.
The government goes along with this because it says once a patient is chronic he does not need so much medical care. So the doctor knows sooner or later he is only going to be able to call on those patients once a week, or charge for it. I notice that calls are down because psychologically that doctor does not want want to picture himself thirty years hence, nor does the nurse. The person who is in the health care field looking after the cleaning or the serving of food does not want to stay too long with an old patient who is declining in health. They do

not want to face the fact that some day they themselves may be in that chair or in that bed.

We must never dispense with that sentiment, Mr. Speaker. It brings a little common sense to some things we do here which are not done right. The shortage of personnel interested and trained in geriatrics is still applicable. This dilemma relates to both the undergraduate and postgraduate levels of medical education. Indeed, somehow the value of the system must be revised so that the care of the chronically ill will be as rewarding as the cure of an acute condition.

I want to refer to the other place. In particular, Senator Croll has done a tremendous amount of work in the Field of aging and humanities, along with other senators. Approximately 20 years ago it was proposed that instead of taking a person's calendar age we should consider his physical and mental age, and people who are physically and mentally able to work should be given the opportunity to carry on. Labour unions as a whole were against that proposal but I think they will eventually reverse their position when it becomes evident that it will be necessary to do so. These labour unions said the proposition was 20 years ahead of its time, that the pill would not have that much effect because not that many people were using it.
It is interesting to note that this subject has been brought up and spurred on by the American Geriatrics Association to the point where a bill has either been passed or is in the process of being passed which will allow people 65 years of age and older, found to be physically and mentally fit, to carry on until they are 70 years of age. This is applicable to the labour classes. In the academic class the bill has gone further by saying that people can carry on as long as they are physically and mentally fit until the age of 90, which brings to mind the man of 95 who was so bright and of whom I spoke earlier. Look at the additional taxation the United States will receive by allowing these people to work.
I know of a medical teacher who retired because the clinic rules were such that retirement was mandatory at age 65. This man was the biggest workhorse I have ever seen. I have seen him start operating at seven o'clock in the morning and carry on until seven o'clock at night. I said to him once: "You are worse than a farmer", and he replied: "I was raised on the farm". At the time he retired he had a pension of $16,000 per year which was quite ample 25 years ago.
In another state because of retirement the seat of professor of surgery was vacant. However, it was tragic that on his way to take up his post the man who was hired died of a coronary. My friend, Pemberton, had been retired for a year at that point and was distraught because he was not working and had decided to do a little general practice, which he did for a short while. In the meantime the clinic knew that my friend was available and even though he was over 65 years of age they said they would hire him if they could find no one better who was younger. He was hired and his post was to be of a year's duration. The year stretched into six years and in that time his salary was in the neighbourhood of $50,000 a year. He was a great man, and I have many fond memories of him. One day I asked him if he liked working this way and he said that it was not for the money he received because the government took almost half of it in tax. He said it is the fact that he was contributing something to this world that had given him so much.

Apparently the federal government is trying to do away with provincial participation in medical research because it no longer believes in confederation but ony in one Unitarian state. If it wishes to ignore them entirely, and make them void by a single stroke of the pen, as though the provinces' opinion did not matter, it should at least be honest enough to return to the provinces the tax points owed to them. I suggest this would at least be logical. One can readily understand that the central government asked for and received the power to collect taxes on behalf of the provinces. That will be profitable for the federal government, but not for our provinces. Mr. Speaker, anybody knows quite well that needs are ever more pressing in the health field and that the provinces will have to foot the bill themselves. Sincerely, is it not another way to punish Quebec? That happened since 1976, especially since that government is there because they do not like it. For example, if I do not like you, will I spend my time throwing things at you? But it is the Quebec people who have elected that government. Why should we punish it continuously and adopt legislation to cut assistance, to break contracts? They even cut back large contracts, the Laprade heavy water plant, for example. It is the same thing. Cutbacks everywhere to try to weaken Quebec's economy.
At the same time the central government gives tax breaks to multinationals, those monopolies which are heavy party fund contributors. This is theoretically to create more jobs, even though we are well aware that large businesses will use the product of the workers' income taxes to modernize and further reduce the number of jobs. That is why big wheels get more
February 7, 1979

powerful under a Liberal government while ordinary folks just get weaker.

Mr. Speaker, I participate in the debate on the bill before the House in a sense of both sorrow and outrage. Earlier the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) said some nice and kind things about the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) with which I agree. There is no question concerning her integrity and desire to improve the lot of Canadians in terms of health care for the aged. She deserves full credit and marks for that. But I question the hon. minister's continuing acquiescence in the priorities of the government and her colleagues. While she may have argued and fought with her cabinet colleagues in caucus concerning restraint being applied to the health resources fund, it seems to me the minister should further attempt to change the minds of her colleagues regarding this legislation. While the minister has been a good trooper in attempting to defend and apologize for this measure, I know her heart is not it.
I am outraged and sorrowful that the minister and her colleagues participated in what I would call a "Proposition 13 syndrome". This mindless pact comes from the Conservative elements in North American society: government is too big, it is spending too much, it interferes too much in our lives, taxes are too high, the government is out of control. It is the restraint policies that are out of control. I never expected to see the day when the hon. minister would be party to such a syndrome or such mindless nonsense emanating from the conservative element in society, smart aleck editorial writers, financial page analysts and so forth.
When analyzing these demands for restraints and cutbacks, one must consider from whom they are coming. One will find that these demands come from the rich, powerful and comfortable. I have not heard any old age pensioners, patients in acute health care beds, veterans, poor people or unemployed say that the government is too big and spends too much money. But 1 have heard such complaints from people who are nicely and comfortably ensconced in $200,000 homes owning two cars, summer cottages and taking winter vacations in California. These kinds of people indicate that the government is too big and its taxes are too high. For any government to accede to such nonsense by placing restraint on health resources expenditures is not only unconscionable, but is giving in to appeals being made to the worst in people rather than the best.
Surely the hon. minister must agree that she should make one more attempt to change the government's mind to its everlasting credit. I see no reason in the government's priorities when displaying restraint on the health of Canadians. The government is cutting $84 million in 1979 and 1980 from health resources funds on the ground of restraint.
The minister said the Government of Canada had a difficult decision to make in applying major traumatic restraint on its own expenditures. I wish the minister would agree-and I do
Health Resources Fund Act
not see how she can fail to-that it must have been more traumatic for her, and everybody else in the cabinet and the Liberal caucus, to hear the government announce an increase in spending just a few days ago of some $400 million, some five times the amount of cutback from the health resources fund, including provision of $18 million to help professional hockey millionaires build places to skate and play their little games. The Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) (Mrs. Campagnolo) tries to justify this by saying they are to be municipally-owned stadiums which will be available to amateurs. I have had some experience of playing amateur hockey with a professional team around, and I know that you can get ice time from seven to eight in the morning or from 11 to midnight, and from midnight until early the next morning. When the professional team wants to use the ice the amateurs and the kids cannot use it. This government can find funds for that.
Why not ask the high-priced players and owners to provide these funds?

That is a good suggestion by the hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski). It would be an excellent idea to have these high-priced players and owners provide their own damned rinks in which to play their games.
What about the announcement of $235 million for the pulp and paper industry? Surely the Minister of National Health and Welfare is not going to hold still for that. She is supposed to knock 84 million bucks from her health resources fund while agreeing to spend $235 million to help an industry that has increased its profits in 12 months from $160 million to $379 million. How can the minister hold still for that? How can any self-respecting Liberal on the government side hold still for that? It is incredible that we have people like the Minister of National Health and Welfare supporting a Liberal government that is implementing Conservative policies. That government not only accedes to the mindless chatter of those who demand restraint and government cutbacks; in its equally mindless desire to clutch and hang on to power it enlarges on those measures. This government has thrown its reputation into disrepute through breaches of faith and word, and its disregard for commitments and agreements with the provinces, beginning in 1966 with the health resources fund.
This program should not be ended prematurely. It should not have $84 million chopped off in its last two years of life. Rather, this program should be extended and enlarged with the provision of new funds, not just $500 million over the next ten years, but $1 billion. There is a great deal yet to be done.
I listened to the words of the learned and fine hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard) who emulates the best traditions of a country doctor in this country. He talked about things that need to be done in a field in which he is wise, the field of geriatrics. I agree with what he said in that regard. I only wish he would talk to his colleagues in his own party in a number of provinces of this country. They have failed miserably to make adequate use or take adequate advantage of the

February 7, 1979
Health Resources Fund Act
health resources fund. Their activities in their own jurisdictions belie the words of the hon. member for Simcoe North.
That hon. member should ask the government of Alberta to refrain from charging $4 a day for medical services for people at levels three and four, most of whom are in what the hon. member for Simcoe North would class the geriatrics category. This is the charge in Alberta to those people who spend more than 120 days in health care centres. He should ask that government to stop collecting $5 a day for the admission of an individual requiring an acute care bed. That government should take full advantage of the health resources fund in order to do more research in geriatrics and to provide a greater degree of medical care through a shared program under the provincial and federal governments. Instead of that Alberta is taxing those who can least afford to pay.
I wish the hon. member would talk to his Conservative colleagues in Ontario who are charging $8.60 a day in what they call extended care user fees. My God, this sounds like Otto Lang! The Tories in Ontario call it a user fee, just as the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) says that the user shall pay. In British Columbia another Conservative government charges $6.50 a day for extended care and $5 a day for acute care. The majority of the people who are paying these charges fall into a category the hon. member for Simcoe North would class as geriatrics.
I hope the hon. member for Simcoe North will match his demands of the federal government with equal demands of his Conservative colleagues in power in several provinces in this country, because their performance in some of the richest provinces, in fact in the richest province, has been shameful and miserly. The government of any province as wealthy as British Columbia, Alberta or Ontario that cannot or will not lead the way in health care and health ventures should be ashamed of itself.
Some of these Conservatives, with a capital "C", talk about more restraint and government cutbacks in health care. Some of them have the nerve to call themselves "Progressive Conservatives", which has to be the ultimate contradiction of terms. They propose things like deterrent fees. We experienced that under a conservative Liberal government in Saskatchewan for a number of years. Dr. Beck, a professor at the University of Saskatchewan, studied the effect of deterrent fees. His findings were that families least able to bear the financial burden cut back on the use of the medical care system. According to Dr. Beck, the wealthy were not noticeably affected. This is what all of us who oppose this kind of tax on the sick have been saying for years.
I would ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare to give more thought to what needs to be done in respect of health care and research rather than to cutbacks. The health resources fund should be extended and enlarged. The $235 million for the pulp and paper industry and the $18 million for hockey rinks should be used to extend and enlarge this fund. It should be used to meet needed research in respect of prosthetics, for the provision of community clinics, acute care for the elderly, for research and the construction of new facilities.

We do not have enough dialysis machines for people with kidney ailments who must have their blood regenerated once or twice a week for the remaining years they have before them. People in the medical profession as a result have to make the terrifying decision of who can have access to the insufficient number of machines and who cannot. We have money for the pulp and paper industry with its high profits and for million-naire hockey club owners, yet the government wants to cut off the health resources fund for its remaining two years.
There are new developments in portable dialysis machines which eliminate the necessity of patients having to attend a hospital once or twice a week year in and year out. Several thousands of these machines are needed and, therefore, the provinces should now spend money on the purchase of these machines and for their continued development with the aid of the federal government, which should absorb half the cost through a health resources fund.
The areas of preventive medicine and mental illness need much research, a high portion of bed occupancy in the health care delivery system is taken up by schizophrenics. The health resources fund could aid in the cost of the work needed in this area. I would like to tell the minister that we could do great things for the improvement and care of schizophrenics and that, if nothing else, it would help half the members of the Liberal party and three quarters of the members in the Conservatives party.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: And all of the NDP.

The Conservative party would like to have it both ways. As my colleague from Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) pointed out with regard to another item some time ago, that party would like to have it both ways. They are like the oldest profession in the world and would like to work both sides of the street. On the one hand they say that there must be cutbacks and restraint, so they pick on the health resources fund; but on the other hand they want to spend three or four times that amount of money on items which have no justification.
Surely the minister will ask her cabinet colleagues and her colleagues in the caucus to readjust their priorities and determine which is the more important-leaving the $84 million in the health resources fund to be spent in 1979 and 1980, or giving $235 million to an industry which has just doubled its profits. That is not dogmatic socialism or party dogma; it is just plain common sense. They must readjust their priorities.
The minister calls the withdrawal of this fund traumatic. Something should be done to ease the trauma. Such a comment indicates to me that she believes it is the wrong decision, because nobody deliberately has a trauma. Why one would want to have a trauma on purpose is beyond me. It is even more traumatic, this decision to end the health resources fund, in light of the spending this government would like to do on unnecessary and unjustified items.
