On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) has been sneering at Alberta for being good and rich and praising Saskatchewan-for being bad and poor, I guess. If that is his thinking, let him explain why such large numbers of people are leaving Saskatchewan and moving to Alberta?

If the hon. member would check the population statistics he would find that such is not the case. But I want to tell him and the natives of Alberta and British Columbia that had it not been for the many good people from Saskatchewan who moved there neither of those places would have amounted to anything.
The fact is that over the last few years in Saskatchewan the population outflow has been reversed. The population has been increasing for the first time since the late 1920s. I do not know whether one can attribute responsibility for that to any party or government, but it does tell one something about where people would prefer to be.
I appeal to the minister to buttonhole a few of her cabinet colleagues. I am sure hon. members of the Conservative party will help keep this debate going until six o'clock, which will give her a chance to change her mind about this bill. After all, ministers over there have already exceeded their objective in connection with cutbacks. They have succeeded without this bill. If it is not proceeded with, they will still be in excess of the objective the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) outlined last September. So they do not need this legislation in order to live up to their commitments about reducing government spending.
I therefore appeal again to the House to reject this legislation. I appeal to the government, to members opposite, and particularly to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. There is nothing wrong about changing your mind if you have second thoughts. You will not be condemned by members of our group if you are big enough to change your mind on this issue. On the contrary, I think you will be applauded by people across this land generally if you withdraw this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is worthwhile, as an introduction to my remarks, to note a statement by the minister. The hon. lady said:
With the impending introduction of a medical care program and anticipated shortages of health manpower to meet program and population requirements for increased health services, the health resources fund was enacted on July 11,
1966, to run for the period 1966-1980.
Provisions of the act were to offer financial assistance to the provinces and territories in the planning, acquisition, construction, renovation and equipping of health training facilities.
Before addressing myself to the remarks made by the minister and statements made before the standing committee dealing with Bill C-2, it is only appropriate that I point out to the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) that in the Barrett era of British Columbia history, if my memory
serves me correctly, a well-known doctor from New Westminster was appointed to draw up a master plan for medical and allied care for that province. Upon its completion it was a ponderous document indeed. It was studied by people within and outside the medical profession and it had much to commend it. But like much socialist philosophy and theory, it suffered from overkill, so much so that this social document for improvement in the field of health gathered dust on the shelves of the provincial legislature in Victoria. I cannot recall one element of that particular tome being introduced by the Barrett government.
I can tell you about all kinds of things.

I would be interested in hearing from the hon. member if he can tell me all kinds of them. Fortunately none was of sufficient significance to have the impact on the province that they are still remarked upon today.
What about dental care for children?

I would suggest to the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre that he address himself to some simple mathematics. I recall him saying that the fee for medical coverage was something like $184 a year in Alberta. That was the figure he quoted-
For a family.

-for a family. When we translate $184 a year, and he mentioned a family of four, it works out to the enormous sum of eight cents a day. Frankly I cannot see anything wrong with that, particularly in Alberta.
It is zero in Saskatchewan.

I know that in Saskatchewan they have a different plan, but times change and governments change. Unless the member is misled, or the House is concerned that the only province which has anything going for it in terms of medical care is Saskatchewan, then I think the member should more fully examine some of the other constraints, such as constraints of environment, population and geography. It is not fair to the other provinces to tar them with a broad brush.
No reference was made to the province of Manitoba. We have a fresh Conservative government there, but the NDP had all kinds of time to establish health care policies. We have not heard a word about that. However, let us return to the substance of the bill instead of debating points between parties here. After all we on the opposition side are opposed to Bill C-2.
In 1966 the prime minister and the government at that time demonstrated considerable foresight in establishing this fund. They must have recognized a need. It is unfortunate they did not demonstrate the foresight to see just what the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) of today and his wasteful wastrels, in other words his cabinet, would do with the financial state of this nation. If he could have seen that, then probably he would

February 7, 1979

have escalated the sum well beyond its present limits. Instead of establishing it at $500 million, maybe he would have established it at $750 million. Perhaps he would have recognized that galloping inflation would diminish the value of the program. Perhaps too he would have considered additional sums were needed to address the social problems that have arisen as a result of the high unemployment in Canada at this time.
The Pearson government did not have that foresight. It did not have the foresight to see what the Prime Minister of today would do. It did not realize that the Prime Minister in a flight of fancy would travel to Bonn, bungle around and then meander to Morocco, and after having been struck by the sun return to Canada to tell the nation that he was fed up with inflation. What the hell is new? What an outstanding statement for the Prime Minister to make! That statement carried about as much credibility as the Prime Minister's statement about wrestling inflation to the ground. The Prime Minister suffers from a sore back. I do not think he has ever made it. Clearly he never will.
I caught the intervention just now of the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk) that the Prime Minister needs a chiropractor. 1 would be delighted to have him as a patient. I cannot say that he would show any immediate response to my treatment; I would rather suspect he would get worse.
The spending of $427 million in the view of the Ministry of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) virtually accomplishes the goal established by the Pearson government. That is not correct. All ministries of this government are suffering from restraint. All programs are suffering from restraint. There are programs which we on this side of the House agree clearly need restraint, but one should not mess around with the health of the nation or its people.
If we could establish a graph of the medical or health care facilities of this nation, that graph would rise from a zero point, or whatever point on the scale one might establish for the year 1966, to a high point in about 1974. From that point on it would stagger; sometimes it would go up and sometimes it would go down. It would go up with the whims of the minister of health in terms of funding the medical research community, and it would drop when the minister decided to extract something from the medical research community. I remember when the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lalonde) discovered $2 million in his pocket for medical research. That graph will now go down and stay down until a Conservative government comes in and changes the ball game. A Conservative government will put the priorities back where they belong.
You will never see that.

On December 12 before the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs I asked the chairman the following question:
-Dr. Law might tell me whether she believes what has happened in the field of medical research, in the field of treatment for disease, in hospitals or out, as it
Health Resources Fund Act
now stands, could have been entirely predicted 15 years ago. Do you believe the current level of medical expertise in the treatment of disease today, thermonuclear medicine or nuclear medicine, for example, could have been predicted 15 years ago? Yes or no? It is that simple. The answer clearly is no.
Dr. Law: I think no.

No, all right. Therefore, do you feel that 15 years from now or 10 years from now we will be at the same level of medical and diagnostic treatment, expertise, that we are at now, that we are not going to advance any further?
Dr. Law: No.

Therefore, would you not say that it is logical to assume that a government, federal government, would consider seriously the continuation of the type of program that is contained within the provisions of this bill.
At that point the Chairman interjected:
I do not know that Dr. Law would wish to answer that question.
I commented that was all right, but the answer is obvious.
What I am trying to demonstrate here is that in spite of the absence of support from this government, research in all fields of the health community must continue. I made reference to nuclear medicine. We are seeing some astounding advances in that field. Those advances will be made to a limited degree in this country because we provide only a very limited degree of support to the scientific community. The advances will be made substantially in those countries which support the scientific community.
In his speech today the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard) dwelt for a considerable time on the subject of geriatrics. He rightfully pointed out that Canadians are living for a longer period of time. There is a desperate need for a more careful and more broadened understanding of the field of geriatrics, as the hon. member for Simcoe North pointed out. The hon. member said in honesty that there are those physicians who feel uncomfortable in the presence and in the treatment of the aged. I can understand that. It seizes their conscience. It is a reflection of the philosophy of today.
When I speak of that, I think of nations such as China, particularly Taiwan or the Republic of China, which carries on with the same philosophy it has had for centuries-respect for parents, grandparents and those most senior in the family. That kind of philosophy has eroded under the communist regime in Red China. It is not appreciated there. That kind of philosophy is in opposition to the state. However, it is still present today in the Republic of China.
That kind of philosophy is also seen in other nations, among other peoples. However, it has rapidly disappeard in this country. As a result, we are faced more and more with the need for extended care facilities, nursing home care and intermediate care. Call it what you may, it deals with the care of the aged and those who are approaching that era of sunset.
These problems are increasing daily. Because of today's society, children are no longer able to cope with their aged parents. They just do not know how. It will take a great deal of time to alter that philosophy. Those kinds of programs will be far reaching, reaching into the next century. We should be thinking of them today. They could well be encompassed in the continuation of this funding and an addition to the funding by means of another bill for an additional $500 million for

February 7, 1979
Health Resources Fund Act
another five, ten or 15 years. At today's prices it would have to be for five years.
There is another area of need that gives me cause for concern. Other members spoke on the subject of care of our Indians. I noticed the interjection of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. She stated the bill did not have anything to do with the provision of medical care in terms of glasses, dentures and so on. That is true. I am not going to discuss that, at least for the moment; I will stick to the bill.
I suggest for her benefit that the minister review an article in the January 4, 1979 Globe and Mail entitled "TB considered serious problem in N.W.T. hamlets". I quote from the article:
Tuberculosis is a serious problem in the community of Rae-Edzo in the Northwest Territories and frustrated health workers are struggling against the disease with only mixed success, a health official says.
At least 48 of the twin hamlet's 1,600 residents are being treated for active tuberculosis and another 102 have been advised to take drugs because they risk developing it, said Dr. Thomas Covill, regional director medical services in the Northwest Territories for the federal Department of Health and Welfare.
Is the minister proud of those statistics? Is she concerned about the fact that for the first time in years we are seeing a rapid increase in the presence of tuberculosis in our Indian communities, a disease which was supposedly wiped out? What is the minister going to do about it? What could this government have done about it if it had taken the opportunity and given direction to the territorial governments, telling them they should be establishing a special clinic or hospital to provide facilities for the treatment of tuberculosis?
What is the tuberculosis rate at Lower Post? Does the minister have any idea how many Indians at Lower Post are afflicted by tuberculosis, how many are carriers and how many are potential carriers? Has anyone in this House heard the minister express any concern about the escalation of tuberculosis among the Indians of Canada? Does the minister know it is a direct reflection of the social conditions in those Indian communities? I have not heard a word from the minister about that. The article continues:
Others who asked not to be named said Dr. Covill's figures are outdated. They put the number of active cases at 57 or more and said more than 300 of the predominantly Indian residents have been told to take anti-TB drugs because of possible contact with the disease.
Dr. Covill acknowledged the incidence of TB is nearly 100 times greater in Rae-Edzo than in most of the rest of Canada. Rae-Edzo is about 80 kilometers northwest of Yellowknife.
In 1977, tuberculosis affected an average of 14.9 of every 100,000 people across Canada. In Rae-Edzo, the incidence was 14.66 of every 1,000.
Not every 100,000.
The situation was the same in the slums of any big city 150 years ago-
I point out to the minister that the situation was the same in the slums of any big city. What is the minister doing about it? Dr. Covill said, and I quote:
"Poor people suffer the disease of poverty and there is nothing medicine can do. Give them an adequate income, decent homes and economic security . .. then you are doing something."

Charlie Charlo, chief of the Rae Indian band and chairman of the Rae-Edzo hamlet council, said at least 20 homes are overcrowded. Many one-room dwellings were inhabited by eight to 16 people.
This is the responsibility of this government, and what has it done about it? It has sat back and waited for the rate of tuberculosis to increase to such a point that it equals the rate of tuberculosis in major cities in Canada 150 years ago, back in the dark ages. The chief said, and I quote:
Some of them may soon move into 18 newly built homes-
What will 18 newly built homes do for a community of 1,600?
But the problem was more complicated than that. Some residents were afraid to ask for treatment and others did not understand they had to take medication for as long as two years rather than just a few days.
Police have arrested known tuberculosis victims who refused treatment.
There lies another problem. If a tuberculosis victim arrested by the police knows his rights, we may well see a problem of confrontation. I agree with the actions of the police, and I am sure all hon. members would; but if a person afflicted with tuberculosis knows his rights, he may well appeal to the Human Rights Commission and say that he was arrested unlawfully.
Because tuberculosis is a communicable disease, it may well be that under certain legislation a person can be held, but he cannot be held indefinitely or until the tuberculosis is cured. At least I do not think so. Are we going to hold people indefinitely so that we can provide medicine for them for two years, and are we going to hold people who come into contact with people who have tuberculosis?
About $84 million is left in a program which has another two years to run. The program could be of enormous benefit in the treatment of tuberculosis, if nowhere else than just among the Indian people in the northern parts of Canada where the disease is most rampant.
I wonder if this government has ever looked at the programs of other nations where indigenous people such as our own Indians are provided with proper hospital care and the level of training needed so that they themselves can treat people of their own race, colour or whatever. Other nations are doing just that. There are provisions for the highest quality medical care and training. Where are the programs here? What kind of program could have been implemented by this insensitive government if it had not tampered with the most valuable element available to anyone, good health?
The minister allowed a few irresponsible people to manage a health care program in Saskatchewan. By her intervention today she demonstrated her frustration with regard to the provision of medical care for our Indians in terms of glasses, dentures and emergency treatment. I respect the minister's intervention because she is right. The matter did not relate directly to the bill, but I think the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk) and our critic on Indian affairs were able to tie it in very nicely with the matters contained in this bill. The hon. member for Athabasca said that abuses are not committed by one group of people or any particular level in society.
February 7, 1979

He cited the experience he has daily working in the emergency ward of an Ottawa hospital.
What kind of department would allow a $12 million deficit in one province because of irresponsible management by officials? Let us make no mistake that it is the province of Saskatchewan which has triggered this reaction by this government. This reaction is the result of irresponsible officials who just did not know how to budget. They could not say no to someone who needed a tenth pair of glasses because the person had been in fights every month of the year. They could not say no to somebody who needed a sixth pair of dentures. They could not say no to somebody who wanted a free ride on an aircraft from La Ronge to Regina so that he could go out and get drunk.
I realize that those are the exceptions and not the rule, but the problem was that the people within the departments concerned, the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and the Department of National Health and Welfare, did not have the guts to say no. As a result, in one province the department was $12 million over budget in one year, last year. We have not heard a word from the government about it.
In the committee, as recorded at page 7:21 of the report for December 12, 1978, the minister said the following:
You want a simple answer, why were the provincial ministers not consulted on my cuts, because they are not elected in the federal portfolio; they have no accountability whatsoever of my budget to any Canadian voter and I really resent the suggestion of the member.
In other words, the minister was telling us that she runs the store and nobody else. There is no consultation, just confrontation. The word "confrontation" is not new to this government.
I heard a beautiful example of confrontation on the radio the other day in Victoria. I suppose the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Anderson) thought no one would hear or recognize his voice. I suppose he thought no one would be able to come back to this House and say that a parliamentary secretary went on the radio publicly and said that the hon. Tom Waterland, a British Columbia minister, is a fool. That is the kind of confrontation problems we have with this government.
It is no wonder the provinces are upset with this government when an irresponsible remark like that is made by a parliamentary secretary. I do not know whether the parliamentary secretary was speaking for his minister; perhaps he was. I have no way of knowing, but he said that clearly. I heard it with my own ears. God knows, I have heard the hon. member's voice in committee enough to recognize his voice. He received a proper introduction, and he said "the minister is a fool", referring to the hon. Tom Waterland. That was confrontation, and the statement by this minister was confrontation.
However, if the Minister of National Health and Welfare wants to run the store, I wonder why she did not tell the province of British Columbia, with reference to the Shau-ghnessy Hospital for Sick Children, that somebody in the provincial department sent her an application but that it was not signed. I wonder why the minister did not indicate that if the province of British Columbia wanted to qualify for assist-
Health Resources Fund Act
ance, it should have had its application in on time and made sure it was signed, and then the federal government would see that the province got the money.
The minister, instead, was very honest with them in Vancouver in June. She told them: "I will be winding down this program, so get in your applications in a hurry". I give the minister full credit for doing so. She told them in advance what was going to happen. They were slow in responding and as a result there will be a $4 million shortfall for the Shau-ghnessy Hospital for Sick Children in Vancouver to be borne by the taxpayers of British Columbia instead of the money coming from this program. It is correct that at least in part the province is responsible for that foul-up, but, after all, the minister herself said on December 12 at a meeting of the committee that she is responsible, that this is a unilateral effort, that the provincial people should not get involved and should not try to tell her what to do, that she is running the store-
"Trying" to run to store.

Yes, as my colleague says, trying to run the store.
I should like to comment on what the minister has had to say, as recorded in the proceedings of December 14 of the Standing Committee on Flealth, Welfare and Social Affairs, at page 8:7. She said:
No, I never said that, Mr. Chairman. My full time is consultation with these bodies. I said that for Bill C-2, I did not consult the provinces, there was no way I could consult the provinces-unfortunately.
She went on to say:
These bodies would have pressed their provincial governments, not the federal government. The initiative rests with the provinces to submit to us whatever projects they want to see us pay for.
That is very true and the minister is correct. But what the minister has failed to do is to reconcile that statement with the other statement she made on December 12 at a meeting of the same committee, when she said that she herself runs the store.
Let me say in conclusion that I will vote against Bill C-2 because there is no question but that health care for Canadians is of prime importance and must continue. I hope that in the next few months we will have an opportunity to introduce our own program which will provide for the concerns that have been mentioned in speeches by members of the House.
I should like to say in closing that my observation of speeches of the minister both in the House and outside the House on television is that at times there is a conflict in what she has said, as was pointed out today by the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen). At the same time, in the words of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), the minister has demonstrated a degree of concern for the poor people of Canada of which I heartily approve. I feel that the minister does indeed have a heart, but I also feel that she is the unfortunate victim of policies inflicted upon the cabinet by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who, returning

February 7, 1979
Health Resources Fund Act
from Morocco, decided, during a heat stroke, to implement a program of restraint. All of a sudden he was smitten with an attack of nausea caused by the bug of inflation and advised the nation that he is fed up. I am just as fed up as the Prime Minister, indeed more, and because I am fed up I welcome the opportunity to vote against this bill and the opportunity, not too far down the road, to defeat this tired government.

Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to have the opportunity to take part in this debate which relates to the fields of science and research with which I have been involved. I will speak about this some time later and bring out some of the specifics of the scientific aspects with which I have been dealing. But let me say first, as many of my colleagues on this side of the House have said before me, that I sincerely sympathize with the minister in her efforts to cover up the shameful cutbacks in medical funds which are outlined in this bill. She stated in her opening speech on third reading of Bill C-2 that:
There was a need to curtail certain levels of planned expenditures in current and future department budgets for which I am responsible,
Instead of saying this, why was it not stated that a directive has come directly from upstairs to cut the expenses down as much as possible and still come up with a program which will make it look as though this was a government of restraint, about which the opposition has been speaking for many years? Why did the minister not say ths was a directive which came out of some of the fuddle-duddled thoughts of her boss who, as my colleague has just said, saw the light all of a sudden? Was it because, as another hon. member said, Proposition 13 was very much in the air at the time? Or was it just the sunshine of Morocco which gave him a heat stroke at a time when the Queen was visiting the country? Possibly it was these thoughts that were going through his mind which prevented the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) from coming back to Canada and being an honourable host when the Queen visited this country to open the Empire Games.
The point I would like to emphasize in reference to Bill C-2 is not that the government has Finally realized that restraint is important, but that its method of imposing this restraint by sudden, arbitrary cuts reflects nothing else but poor management of the whole situation. This was discussed briefly by my colleague, the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Graff-tey), but allow me to elaborate in a few words.
Back on November 21, in my maiden speech to the House, I spoke on the subject of management in government circles. In addition to some nine years of studies into biochemical and nutritional science techniques, I have been involved, since I left the research field, with business circles for the last 20 years. I pointed out in my speech that good management must apply in government just as in business. The businessman who uses poor management and ends up with deficits year after year ends up in bankruptcy. This is just what is happening to the present government, and this is what is going to happen to Canada.
The restraints being put into effect by the federal government now are very much needed, as they have been over the

last eight or ten years, but the fact should have been realized before this program was started in 1966. The inability to plan and to manage of the Trudeau government is now showing up, and all of a sudden savings must be made and spending cuts applied in a hurry. So we see the band-aid efforts that are in effect. This is the difference between good and bad government. Just as in business, a good government looks ahead and plans on a total financial basis for many years ahead, through wise judgment and planning on the part of wise, conscientious and knowledgeable politicians and administrators. They utilize their experience and wisdom to plan the best methods of achieving optimum results.
A bad government, on the other hand, gives little thought to the future. The plans and the budget are only loosely coordinated. There is little planning and there is little thought for optimization of finances and the ensuing results. This is the present state of affairs as it applies to Bill C-2. The years of poor planning and mismanagement of the present government have caught up to it, and now the country is in deep trouble. It is easy merely to take a pencil and erase figures in the budget for the immediate future. That would provide a turnaround; it is a very simple financial transaction. But even in the planning of such restraint, thought must be given to a method of maximizing the value of dollars being spent. This should have been done by the present Liberal government ten years ago, and it should have been continued as years went by.
At a time when dollar efficiency must be maximized, certainly it is a sign of poor management to cut research dollars. Surely a decrease of 17 per cent in the original research expenditure on short notice shocked those involved in the program. It is relatively easy to cut straightforward spending programs on a short notice basis, but research is an area which requires time to plan the general research program and to train personnel whose backgrounds are precise and specific. Also the necessary equipment for research is complex and costly. This area requires careful study to ensure optimum dollar effectiveness. Optimum returns to dollar expenditure may be realized in the area of research.
The ramifications of the proposed cut in medical funding portends grave implications for the quality of future health care in Canada. Largely, medical research is carried out under the auspices of universities and medical schools where the doctors of tomorrow learn the specialized skills of their professions. There is a direct link between research and practice in the field of medicine. Both are conducted under the same roof and reinforce each other. Any cut in medical funding lowers the standard of medical education which cannot help but result in diminished standards of medical care. The reductions in medical research caused by cuts in government funding in many instances will deprive physicians and surgeons of the consultation they require to perform their functions. In life and death situations good advice is crucial, and such good advice does not come cheaply. Yes, it is expensive but necessary. Fiscal restraint is not justified when the fate of a patient
February 7, 1979

on the operating table is at stake. Practising doctors need the advice of researchers. Without it, severe limitations are placed on their capabilities.
The proposed cuts will have geographic implications as well. In the past, the lion's share of medical research funds went to institutions in Montreal, Ottawa and Toronto. Newer facilities in western Canada, which commenced the development of research units in the past five to ten years, will feel the pinch of such cuts proportionately more than medical institutions and schools in central Canada. Cutbacks will have a devastating effect upon programs which are just getting off the ground.
Canada has lagged behind other countries in the provisions of funds for medical research. For example, the United States spent more than $1 billion in 1978 alone, and that is only its federal government funding. The annual federal allocations in Canada pale in comparison to those in the United States. In 1978, some $63 million was expended by the Department of National Health and Welfare, and now we are faced with a cut in the health resources fund which will reduce medical spending by $84 million.
The bill we are discussing at the present time is a very important one, as spending in medical research and development is a large and significant factor when one considers the total dollar spending of government.
The cuts will have serious effects upon the quality of people in medical schools. Young medical researchers are most attracted to research institutes and universities offering opportunities to conduct high quality research in their areas of precise scientific and medical studies. These opportunities are reduced when medical research funds are cut by government. In that event medical researchers are obliged to look elsewhere, such as to the United States which seems wiser in this area and sees fit to support health research on a scale heretofore unknown in Canada. Is the government prepared to see an
Health Resources Fund Act
exodus of our best doctors and students south of the border? How much will it cost to recoup the actual and potential loss of medical knowledge and progress, which almost certainly will result from an $84 million cut? Is this the beginning of a trend whereby it will be necessary to import medical breakthroughs because the government blocked research money which would allow them to happen in Canada? Will we have de-medicalization as well as de-industrialization? My party has never been more serious in opposing a bill and its ramifications for the Canadian public than it is now.
The rationale of the quick change in thinking of the Prime Minister abruptly altered the lives of a great many Canadians. Perhaps it would not be so bad if it did not apply to the health of individual citizens. In one of the contributions on this side of the House, it was mentioned that the cost of polio research was only $41 million. The savings brought about by this one simple discovery amounted to over $200 million per year in Canada alone. How much money has this $41 million expenditure saved other countries around the world?
Polio is only one example. All members are aware of the efforts of one of Canada's foremost research teams in the years subsequent to the First World War. I am referring to Drs. Banting and Best who discovered insulin at the University of Toronto. Although the cost of that discovery was negligible, it saved Canada a large amount of money because now insulin is available for diabetics. Also it saved billions of dollars around the world.
As it is now six o'clock and I have further material to present, Mr. Speaker, I trust I may continue tomorrow.
